questions.question: Why is my function sometimes returning none instead of a number that's expected?
questions.expected_answer: Some code path in your function finishes without returning a number, so Python implicitly returns None. Common causes: an if/elif branch with no else (or no return after it), a recursive call whose result is not returned, returning the result of a method that returns None (such as list.sort() or list.append()), or an explicit bare return / return None on one path. Make sure every possible path returns the expected value.

questions.question: Why am I having trouble understanding shallow and deep copies?
questions.expected_answer: A shallow copy creates a new object but references the same elements as the original object. A deep copy creates a new object and recursively copies all elements of the original object.

questions.question: If I create a variable inside a Python function and then try to use that variable outside the function. Will the variable still be available? Explain why or why not.
questions.expected_answer: No. A variable assigned inside a function is local to that function's scope: it exists only while the function runs, so using its name outside the function raises a NameError. Returning it hands back the value (not the variable itself), which the caller can store in its own variable. The main exception is declaring the variable global inside the function, which makes it a module-level variable.

questions.question:
What is the exact output of the following Python 3 code? Explain why it does not match the 'expected' rounding result of 2.68.

print(round(2.675, 2))
questions.expected_answer: 2.67 -- not because of banker's rounding, but because 2.675 cannot be represented exactly in IEEE 754 double-precision floating point. The actual stored value is approximately 2.67499999999999982236..., which is strictly less than 2.675, so round() correctly rounds down to 2.67.

questions.question:
What is the exact output of this Python 3 function call? Explain what happens to the return value from the try block.

def f():
    try:
        return 1
    finally:
        return 2

print(f())
questions.expected_answer: 2 -- when a finally block contains its own return statement, it unconditionally overrides any return, exception, or break/continue propagating out of the try block. The try's 'return 1' begins to execute but is discarded once the finally block's 'return 2' runs. (Python 3.14 also emits a SyntaxWarning on stderr for a return inside finally, per PEP 765, but the program's output is still 2.)
questions.expected_output_code:
def f():
    try:
        return 1
    finally:
        return 2
print(f())
# Output: 2

questions.question: What is a segmentation fault and how do I prevent it in my code?
questions.expected_answer: A segmentation fault is a runtime error that occurs when a program tries to access a memory location it is not allowed to access, or tries to access it in a way that is forbidden (for example, writing to read-only memory). Common causes are dereferencing a null or uninitialized pointer, using a dangling pointer (memory that was already freed, or a local variable that has gone out of scope), going out of bounds on an array or vector, and infinite recursion that overflows the stack. To prevent it: initialize pointers and check for nullptr before dereferencing, never return or keep pointers/references to local variables, do not use memory after delete/free, check array and vector bounds (for example with .at()), prefer smart pointers and standard containers over raw new/delete, and use tools such as AddressSanitizer, Valgrind, or a debugger like gdb to find the faulting access.

questions.question: What are the pros of not using a destructor when using dynamic memory?
questions.expected_answer: There are no real pros to not using a destructor when using dynamic memory. If a class owns memory allocated with new and has no destructor that deletes it, that memory is never released when the object is destroyed, which is a memory leak (a leak is not undefined behavior by itself, but the program keeps wasting memory and can eventually run out of it). It is important to manage dynamic memory properly by implementing a destructor that frees the allocated memory (and, if you do, also handling copying correctly: the Rule of Three/Five), or by using smart pointers such as std::unique_ptr so that cleanup is automatic.

questions.question: Two algorithms have the same time complexity, but one consistently finishes faster than the other. Why can this happen?
questions.expected_answer: Time complexity (Big-O) only describes how the running time grows as the input size grows; it ignores constant factors and lower-order terms. Two algorithms with the same time complexity can still finish at different times because of different constant factors and lower-order terms (for example 2n vs 5n operations), implementation details (language, compiler optimizations, data structures, function-call overhead), memory access patterns and cache behavior, the particular input being tested (best, average, or worst case), and the hardware or system load at the time of measurement.
The time complexity of this code is O(n log n).

questions.question: In a binary search tree, what happens if you insert the values 10, 5, 15, 3, 7, 12, 18 in that order? What would an in-order traversal output?
questions.expected_answer: 10 becomes the root; 5 and 15 become its left and right children; 3 and 7 go under 5, and 12 and 18 go under 15, giving a perfectly balanced tree (smaller values go left, larger values go right). An in-order traversal (left, node, right) of a BST always visits the values in sorted order: 3 5 7 10 12 15 18.

questions.question: You are given an unweighted graph. Which algorithm should you use to find the shortest path between two nodes, BFS or DFS? Explain why. I need the answer quick
questions.expected_answer: BFS should be used because it explores nodes level by level and guarantees the shortest path in an unweighted graph. DFS does not guarantee the shortest path.

questions.question: Difference between bubble sort and selection sort?
questions.expected_answer: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are out of order, so the largest remaining element bubbles to the end on each pass (this can take many swaps). Selection sort scans the unsorted part for the smallest element and swaps it into its correct position, using at most one swap per pass (n-1 swaps total). Both are O(n^2) in the worst case.
